items.title: DEP: Extract the mocker scheduler simulation core into a reusable crate [DYN-3589]

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Summary

Extract the synchronous, per-worker scheduler simulation core from `dynamo-mocker` into an independently versioned Rust crate that can be consumed by both Dynamo and AIC.

The extracted crate should model vLLM-, SGLang-, and TensorRT-LLM-style scheduling, G1 KV-cache residency, request lifecycle, and deterministic per-pass execution without depending on `dynamo-kv-router`, `kvbm-*`, AIC, Tokio, or any Dynamo live-runtime type. G1 should return to an explicit reference-counted cache with a deterministic LRU inactive pool, based on the pre-#8451 mocker implementation. Router publication, KVBM tier simulation, tracing, and performance models should attach through project-neutral traits or domain effects with no-op implementations available to consumers that do not need them.

Phase 1 intentionally does **not** migrate either runtime that drives the core:

- Dynamo's live async waiter/runtime stays in the Dynamo repository.
- Dynamo's virtual-time offline replay harness, including single-worker, multi-worker, scaling, router modes, trace collection, and disaggregated replay, also stays in the Dynamo repository.

Both become consumers of the extracted synchronous core. A later proposal can reconsider whether any replay components should move after the core boundary has stabilized.

This DEP is intended to open an architecture and ownership discussion. It does not authorize or prescribe an immediate code move.

## Motivation

`dynamo-mocker` currently combines several layers with different ownership and dependency needs:

1. Synchronous engine scheduling and G1 cache simulation.
2. Dynamo-specific router protocols and KV event publication.
3. KVBM G1/G2/G3/G4 integration.
4. Live async execution, including Tokio channels, waiters, wall-clock sleeps, cancellation, and publisher services.
5. Deterministic virtual-time offline replay and trace reporting.
6. CLI, Python bindings, workload loaders, and deployment integration.

That combination makes the scheduler simulation difficult to reuse outside Dynamo. The crate has unconditional dependencies on `dynamo-kv-router`, `dynamo-tokens`, and `kvbm-logical`. The vLLM scheduler core directly stores `kvbm_logical::MutableBlock` and `ImmutableBlock`; pass results and lifecycle effects carry `dynamo_kv_router::protocols::RouterEvent`; event sinks accept Dynamo router protocol types; admissions can be sent through Tokio channels; and the core calls the replay `TraceCollector` directly.

This is a poor boundary for AIC. AIC needs the scheduler's request admission, batching, preemption, KV-capacity, prefix-reuse, and forward-pass behavior, but should not need Dynamo's router, KVBM, event transports, live worker runtime, or replay implementation. Copying the scheduler into AIC would create two implementations that drift. Depending on all of `dynamo-mocker` would pull in unrelated runtime dependencies and make crate ownership and releases circular.

The G1 implementation also has a historical seam worth restoring. Before #8451, mocker used a small `HashCache` with explicit per-block reference counts and an `LRUEvictor` for inactive blocks. #8451 replaced it with `kvbm-logical::BlockManager<G1>`, after which mocker added a substantial adapter and shadow registries to translate KVBM's RAII and lineage model back into scheduler and router semantics. Today `kvbm_backend.rs` is over 3,000 lines and mixes baseline G1 behavior, router event construction, block-hash translation, destination reservations, and optional offload behavior. KVBM remains valuable for Dynamo's tiered offload experiments, but it should not define the baseline scheduler simulation's G1 ownership model.

## Proposal

### 1. Establish a strict phase-1 ownership boundary

Create a project-neutral Rust crate, referred to as `scheduler-sim-core` in this DEP. The final name and repository are open questions.

| Reusable `scheduler-sim-core` crate | Remains in Dynamo |
| --- | --- |
| Synchronous vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM scheduler cores and policies | Live Tokio scheduler/waiter wrappers |
| Neutral request, output, lifecycle, cache, FPM, and pass-effect types | Channels, cancellation tokens, wall-clock sleeps, readiness/session tasks |
| Manual vLLM G1 cache and SGLang radix-cache simulation | KVBM G2/G3/G4 engines and Dynamo offload adapters |
| Request/sequence state, speculative decode, and handoff state machines needed by one worker | KV router protocol conversion and event publication |
| Project-neutral latency/cache/offload/observation seams | ZMQ/NATS/runtime publishers and services |
| Synchronous `submit`, `apply_command`, and `execute_pass` APIs | Entire offline replay harness and trace collector/reporting |
| Deterministic per-worker pass effects | CLI, PyO3, workload parsing, progress, deployment wiring |

The extracted crate must not depend on:

- any `dynamo-*` crate;
- any `kvbm-*` crate;
- `aiconfigurator-core` or other AIC implementation crates;
- Tokio, `tokio-util`, transport libraries, or Dynamo runtime crates.

Small general-purpose crates such as `serde`, `uuid`, `rand`, `rustc-hash`, or `anyhow` are acceptable where they materially simplify the public API.

### 2. Restore a standalone manual G1 cache

Replace `kvbm-logical::BlockManager<G1>` as the baseline vLLM G1 manager with a focused cache owned by the reusable crate. The historical pre-#8451 `HashCache`, `vllm_backend`, and `LRUEvictor` provide the starting semantics, but the implementation should be rewritten against current scheduler behavior rather than copied blindly.

The minimum state is:

- an active map from a neutral block key to an explicit non-zero request reference count;
- a partial-block map for request-owned blocks that have not been promoted;
- an inactive LRU containing resident blocks with zero request references;
- fixed block capacity and block size;
- enough neutral metadata to emit cache transition effects and preserve parent-chain/token information when a consumer requests it.

The observable lifecycle remains:

1. `Use`: increment an active reference, reactivate an inactive block, or evict the least-recently-used inactive block and allocate a miss.
2. `Deref`: decrement the explicit reference count and move the block to inactive LRU when it reaches zero.
3. `Promote`: replace a request-owned partial block with a full block, coalescing a collision onto the existing cache entry.
4. Cleanup/cancel: release only references owned by that request and preserve deterministic eviction ordering.

The migration must characterize and preserve scheduler-visible behavior around partial allocation, shared-prefix references, preemption/recomputation, promotion collisions, disabled prefix caching, destination reservation, and cache store/remove timing. The discussion should explicitly decide whether preempted blocks require a `push_front` eviction priority or ordinary LRU insertion; this must be driven by observable scheduler parity tests rather than an assumption.

KVBM no longer owns G1 in the baseline simulator. Dynamo may still attach KVBM-backed lower-tier/offload behavior through an extension seam.

### 3. Replace Dynamo protocol types with neutral effects and traits

The core should never construct or expose `KvCacheEvent`, `RouterEvent`, `StorageTier`, `WorkerId`, or `KvRouterConfig`.

Define project-neutral domain types and seams, for example:

- `BlockKey`, `LocalBlockKey`, and optional parent/position metadata;
- `CacheEvent::{Stored, Removed, Cleared}`;
- `CacheTier` expressed as a neutral identifier or associated type;
- `PassEffects` containing admissions, output tokens, lifecycle events, cache events, and FPM snapshots;
- a `LatencyModel` interface used by scheduler timing;
- an optional `OffloadBackend` interface with an inert `NoopOffload` implementation;
- an observation/event sink that can be `Noop` in AIC and adapted to Dynamo publishers.

Prefer buffered effects returned by `execute_pass` or statically dispatched generic sinks over dynamic calls on every token. This keeps the no-op path cheap and lets Dynamo's live and replay drivers consume the same effects.

Dynamo implements adapters that:

- map neutral block identities and cache events to Dynamo token/hash and router protocol types;
- publish live events through the existing sinks;
- feed offline cache events to the synchronous Dynamo KV router when KV-aware replay is selected;
- attach KVBM offload simulation when a Dynamo run requests G2/G3/G4 behavior;
- translate core admissions/tokens/FPMs into the existing live and replay consumers.

AIC uses the same core with `NoopOffload` and either ignores cache publication effects or installs a small metrics observer. AIC should not need fake Dynamo `RouterEvent` values merely to step the scheduler.

Block identity and hashing need an explicit contract. The recommended direction is a neutral key/hasher interface so the reusable crate has no source dependency on `dynamo-tokens`: Dynamo supplies its exact production-compatible hash adapter, while AIC may use a deterministic default whose equality and prefix-chain behavior are sufficient for simulation.

### 4. Keep both driver runtimes in Dynamo

The extracted API is synchronous:

```text
submit(request)
apply_command(command)
execute_pass(now_ms) -> PassEffects
next_internal_deadline() -> Option<f64>
```

It must not own:

- an async task or runtime;
- request/output channels;
- wall-clock waiting or precision sleep loops;
- cancellation tokens;
- readiness/session publisher tasks;
- ZMQ/NATS/event-plane code;
- a virtual-time cluster event loop;
- routing across workers;
- workload admission, trace collection, or report generation.

Dynamo retains two separate drivers:

1. The live `Scheduler`/`SglangScheduler` wrappers translate Tokio channels, cancellation, publishers, and wall-clock behavior into synchronous core calls.
2. The existing offline replay harness translates its virtual clock, event heap, worker pools, routers, scaling, disaggregated handoff orchestration, and `TraceCollector` into synchronous core calls.

Admissions currently sent through a Tokio channel and observations currently written directly into `TraceCollector` should instead appear in `PassEffects`. This is necessary even though neither driver migrates: it prevents the reusable core from depending on either driver.

### Scheduler semantic prerequisites

Extraction must preserve a stable scheduler contract rather than move ambiguous behavior across the crate boundary. Before extraction, ordinary `MoveBlock::Use` must satisfy the transactional contract in [#11016](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11016): a failed plan is invisible to active refs, cache reuse, sequence state, and emitted cache effects; typed outcomes distinguish capacity exhaustion, concrete offload dependency, and bounded immediate retry. Ordinary and speculative decode consume the same contract.

This is a characterization and parity gate for extraction, not a second implementation scope. Explicit disaggregated source/destination reservations remain owned by [#10736](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/10736). Replay liveness classification remains in [#11015](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11015), and asynchronous KVBM settlement remains in [#11018](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11018).

### 5. Make the current offline harness the phase-1 parity consumer

Although replay does not move, it is the strongest validation surface for the extraction. Dynamo's existing single-worker, multi-worker round-robin, KV-router, scaling, and disaggregated modes should continue to run against the extracted core.

The replay event heap is not scheduler-core state. It exists to order communication among simulated components: worker completions change load before closed-loop backfill/admission; cache events update router state before later placements; and transfers, worker startup, or scaling schedule future state changes. If AIC phase 1 directly steps one or more cores and supplies admission decisions itself, it does not need that coordination machinery. Shared replay becomes worth reconsidering when AIC needs the same cross-worker closed-loop causality, KV-event-driven routing, load tracking, or disaggregated handoff ordering as Dynamo.

Phase-1 parity gates should compare the pre- and post-extraction core through the existing harness for:

- single-worker trace and concurrency replay;
- one-worker aggregate-harness equivalence with the single-worker path;
- deterministic multi-worker round-robin dispatch and timing;
- vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM scheduler modes;
- prefix-cache hits, preemption, chunked prefill, speculative decode, and FPMs;
- disaggregated source/destination lifecycle and transfer timing;
- KV-aware and KVBM-enabled Dynamo modes through adapters.

These tests validate the shared core boundary without making replay API design part of phase 1. A later DEP can decide whether AIC needs a shared cluster replay harness after it has exercised the per-worker API directly.

### 6. Consumption and repository direction

The desired dependency direction is:

```text
AIC -----------------> scheduler-sim-core
Dynamo live ---------> scheduler-sim-core
Dynamo offline replay -> scheduler-sim-core
                            ^
                            no dependency on either consumer
```

Dynamo's `dynamo-mocker` crate becomes a compatibility facade and integration crate. Existing Python, Rust, live, and replay entrypoints remain stable while their per-worker scheduling work delegates to `scheduler-sim-core`.

The crate must be independently versioned and consumable without checking out Dynamo. Because Dynamo already depends on `aiconfigurator-core`, placing the only reusable source inside Dynamo and making AIC depend back on it creates source and release-cycle friction. The preferred options are:

1. publish/host the crate from the AIC repository, with no dependency on AIC implementation crates; or
2. publish/host it from a small independent repository owned jointly by the Dynamo/AIC maintainers.

Keeping it in the Dynamo repository can still work only if it is published independently and AIC consumes a released crate rather than creating a source dependency cycle. Repository, crate name, release cadence, and code ownership are explicit decisions for this DEP.

### 7. Suggested phase-1 migration slices

These are discussion slices, not an approved implementation plan:

1. Add characterization tests for current scheduler and manual-cache target semantics using the existing offline harness.
2. Introduce neutral pass/cache/lifecycle effects and stop the scheduler core from calling `TraceCollector`, sending Tokio admissions, or constructing router protocol types.
3. Restore the manual G1 reference-count/LRU manager and keep KVBM offload behind a Dynamo adapter.
4. Extract request/sequence state, scheduler policies, vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM cores, and their direct unit tests.
5. Integrate the released crate in AIC and make both Dynamo drivers delegate to it.
6. Remove duplicated compatibility code only after live and offline parity/performance gates pass.

## Alternate Solutions

### Keep one `dynamo-mocker` crate and use Cargo feature flags

A `core` feature could turn off KVBM and router code. This reduces initial file movement but does not establish a clean API or release boundary. Current core types already mention Dynamo router, replay, and KVBM types, so feature flags alone would produce a fragile matrix of `cfg` branches. It also leaves AIC coupled to Dynamo's repository and release cadence.

### Keep `kvbm-logical` as G1 and hide it behind a trait

This avoids rewriting the cache manager, but baseline simulation would still inherit KVBM ownership, identity, and RAII semantics. AIC would pay for and stub an abstraction whose only implementation is a Dynamo-specific block manager. It also preserves the large translation layer that motivated the extraction.

### Copy the scheduler code into AIC

This gives AIC immediate control but creates two schedulers. Behavior will drift as Dynamo adds scheduler parity, handoff, or cache fixes. Cross-project validation becomes comparison rather than shared implementation.

### Move all of `dynamo-mocker` into AIC

This would move too much. The live waiter, offline replay harness, Dynamo router integration, KVBM offload, transports, CLI, bindings, and deployment behavior are Dynamo concerns. AIC should own or consume a scheduler simulation library, not Dynamo's mock backend runtime.

### Include the offline replay harness in phase 1

A shared replay harness may eventually be useful, but its event heap is specifically coordination machinery for cross-component causality: closed-loop admission timing after worker completions, KV-event and load-state propagation into later routing decisions, scaling/startup events, and disaggregated handoff timing. Those needs broaden the first boundary substantially. Phase 1 instead keeps replay in Dynamo as a parity consumer; migration should be reconsidered only when AIC needs those same interactions rather than direct per-core stepping.

## Requirements

- The reusable crate compiles and tests without Dynamo, KVBM, AIC, Tokio, or replay-harness dependencies in its graph.
- Dynamo's live async waiter/runtime remains in the Dynamo repository and preserves its current external behavior.
- Dynamo's complete offline replay harness remains in the Dynamo repository in phase 1.
- AIC can construct, submit to, command, and step a scheduler core with no Dynamo router, KVBM, live-runtime, or replay stubs.
- The core G1 manager uses explicit reference counts and deterministic inactive LRU eviction.
- Neutral effects preserve all information needed for Dynamo to publish compatible KV events and collect replay metrics outside the core.
- Scheduler behavior is characterized for vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM modes before migration.
- Existing Dynamo live, single-worker replay, multi-worker replay, KV-router replay, and disaggregated replay continue to pass through adapters.
- Hot paths do not require dynamic dispatch per token when a generic or batched-effect interface is sufficient.
- KVBM-enabled and KV-router-enabled Dynamo modes remain possible through adapters and are validated separately from the independent baseline.
- Benchmarks compare per-pass runtime and allocation overhead before and after extraction using the existing replay benchmarks.
- Existing Dynamo Python/CLI entrypoints remain compatibility surfaces during migration.

## Open Questions

1. Should the crate live in AIC, a neutral repository, or Dynamo with independent publication?
2. What is the minimum public scheduler API AIC needs in phase 1 beyond `submit`, `apply_command`, and `execute_pass`?
3. Which FPM and lifecycle schemas belong in the reusable core, and which remain consumer adapters?
4. What is the smallest neutral block identity/hasher contract that preserves Dynamo router compatibility without depending on `dynamo-tokens`?
5. Does KVBM tier simulation implement a generic `OffloadBackend`, remain entirely above the scheduler core, or require a smaller set of reservation/deadline hooks?
6. Which historical LRU/preemption ordering is the intended observable contract: ordinary LRU, explicit preemption-priority insertion, or a selectable policy?
7. Which request/handoff features are truly per-worker core semantics versus Dynamo driver policy?
8. Who owns release compatibility and cross-repository CI for the shared crate?
9. Which concrete AIC use case first requires a shared event heap: closed-loop admission timing, KV-event/load-aware routing, scaling, or disaggregated handoff?

## References

- [Current vLLM scheduler core](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/333b15682fafc60329793b61185e5f30c0a915c4/lib/mocker/src/scheduler/vllm/core.rs)
- [Current KVBM-backed G1 manager](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/333b15682fafc60329793b61185e5f30c0a915c4/lib/mocker/src/kv_manager/kvbm_backend.rs)

items.title: fix(llm): normalize tool_call arguments from JSON string to object before template render
items.body:
## Summary

GLM-5.2's Jinja chat template calls `.items()` on `tool_calls[*].function.arguments`, expecting a dict. The OpenAI wire format carries arguments as a JSON string. In multi-turn conversations where the assistant's previous turn contained tool calls, the template renderer receives a string where it expects a dict, producing empty or garbled argument output.

**Before** (arguments as JSON string passed to the template):
```
template sees: tc.function.arguments = '{"path": "/tmp/foo"}'
.items() on a string → empty iteration
rendered:      <tool_call>read_file</tool_call>
```

**After** (arguments normalized to a dict before the template):
```
template sees: tc.function.arguments = {"path": "/tmp/foo"}
.items() works correctly
rendered:      <tool_call>read_file<arg_key>path</arg_key><arg_value>/tmp/foo</arg_value></tool_call>
```

This matches TRT-LLM's behavior: `chat_utils.py` always calls `json.loads(arguments)` before `apply_chat_template` when the value is a string. No template detection or thread-local plumbing is needed — `normalize_tool_call_arguments()` is called unconditionally in `messages()` for all three `OAIChatLikeRequest` implementors (`NvCreateChatCompletionRequest`, `UnifiedRequest`, `SpeculativePrefillRequest`). Non-object and malformed-JSON values are replaced with `{}` with a warning (byte length only — no raw content in logs).

items.body:
<!-- codex-pr-description:start -->
This exposes agent identity and effective agent hints through `WorkerSelectionContext`. Custom worker scorers and pickers can now use request intent without adding another worker-signal group or changing default selection behavior.

### How This Was Implemented
- Let `WorkerSelectionContext` privately borrow the existing `SchedulingRequest`.
- Add direct getters for session ID, expected output tokens, priority jump, and strict priority.
- Cover the custom picker path with a unit test.

<details>
<summary>Walkthrough</summary>

#### Mental model

The router already normalizes agent metadata before worker selection. This change makes the scheduler-resident subset available to every custom scorer and picker through their existing context argument.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Agent request] --> B[SchedulingRequest]
    B --> C[WorkerSelectionContext]
    C --> D[Custom scorer or picker]
```

#### Request lifecycle

`WorkerSelectionInput::new` stores one private reference to the existing scheduling request. Scorers and pickers read its agent-derived fields through direct context getters; no metadata is copied and no policy state or worker-row allocation is added.

#### Boundaries and limitations

Default EPP selection is unchanged because the default scorer and picker do not call the new getters. The context exposes only agent data already carried by `SchedulingRequest`; transport-only fields such as parent-session lifecycle metadata and speculative-prefill hints are not newly plumbed through the KV router.

</details>

- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-kv-router --all-targets -- -D warnings`

items.title: fix(mocker): model SGLang KV allocation by page
items.body:
## Overview

The SGLang mocker currently allocates and retains individual token-slot IDs even though SGLang's paged allocator owns and frees whole pages. This undercounts active partial-page occupancy, retains per-token metadata in the completed radix cache, and can produce capacity and eviction behavior that the real allocator cannot.

## Motivation

Offline replay maintains an independent SGLang radix tree for every simulated worker. On large production traces, retaining a token-slot ID for every token in every completed cached page makes the radix-tree memory footprint grow with both cached tokens and worker count; this became the dominant memory cost in high-worker-count Astra replay runs. Completed pages only need page/block identity, so this PR replaces that unnecessary per-token state with compact per-page metadata while preserving SGLang allocator semantics.

## Summary

- Replace the token-slot pool with a whole-page allocator while preserving flattened token indices only for bounded active requests.
- Store one router-compatible block hash and one physical page ID per completed radix page instead of per-token IDs.
- Make prefill, decode, destination reservations, eviction, retraction, and worker KV metrics account for physical page ownership.
- Protect a matched prefix before eviction and allocation, avoiding a false-OOM race when the matching prefix is the LRU victim.
- Hash and validate only the newly completed suffix during retained-prefix insertion, avoiding quadratic decode growth.

## Details

Completed radix edges now retain `LocalBlockHash + KvPageId` per page. Active partial pages consume their full physical capacity and extend in place until the page boundary; decode reserves new pages only when a request crosses that boundary. Finished partial tails release the entire page, while complete pages remain compactly indexed in the radix tree.

The 64-bit local block hash is intentionally the page identity, matching router-side indexing. Hash collisions are therefore treated as identical pages, rather than retaining an exact per-token collision guard.

At constrained capacity, replay results can intentionally differ from the previous mocker because unused positions in an active partial page are no longer exposed as allocatable capacity.

## Where should the reviewer start?

- `lib/mocker/src/cache/radix_cache.rs`: `PagePool`, compact radix representation, suffix-only insertion, and page-granular eviction.
- `lib/mocker/src/kv_manager/sglang_backend.rs`: request ownership, atomic match/protect/evict/allocate, decode and destination reservations, canonicalization, and router events.
- `lib/mocker/src/scheduler/sglang/{prefill,decode,core}.rs`: page-aware admission, reservation, and KV usage accounting.

items.title: DEP: Refactor DGDR profiler to use Dynamo Replay

labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Summary

Refactor the DGDR profiler to use Dynamo Replay as its deployment-level simulation and search engine. AIConfigurator (AIC) will provide forward-pass performance estimates and memory-fit estimates, Replay will simulate Dynamo deployment behavior including scheduling, replicas, routing, planner decisions, and traffic dynamics, and the DGDR profiler will orchestrate parallel configuration sweeps. The profiler will return a ranked set of viable deployment candidates and artifacts, not only a single best configuration, so users can inspect the recommendation, alternatives, constraints, replay report, and whether the recommendation is advisory or auto-applied.

## Motivation

The current DGDR profiler can generate optimal engine configurations only for static traffic assumptions. This leaves two major gaps. First, important Dynamo components such as the router and planner have complex configuration surfaces, but the profiler does not model or optimize them. Second, static traffic is not representative of real serving workloads, where request arrival patterns, sequence lengths, burstiness, cache locality, and multi-turn behavior can materially change the best deployment configuration.

The current DGDR profiler, mocker/replay stack, and AIC also each maintain some performance-modeling or sweep logic. We should make the component boundaries explicit to reduce duplicated work. AIC should focus on forward-pass time estimation. Mocker and Replay should compose AIC estimates with scheduler, multi-replica, router, planner, and deployment simulation to act as a fast digital twin of Dynamo deployments. The DGDR profiler should sit above Replay and add search-space construction, optimization, and DGDR-compatible output generation.

## Proposal

Use Dynamo Replay as the profiling backend for DGDR optimization. Replay already supports CPU-based virtual-time deployment simulation, static and dynamic traffic inputs, offline execution, and router/planner configuration. Replay is also already integrated with AIC-backed timing surfaces, with ongoing work to expose a Rust forward-pass API.

The DGDR user experience should remain largely unchanged. Users continue to submit a DGDR with model, hardware, backend, SLA, and deployment intent. Existing static traffic inputs remain supported as the backward-compatible default. The primary UX addition is a dynamic workload input contract.

Dynamic workload input should support four levels of input, all normalized by the profiler into Replay-ready workload artifacts:

- Replay-ready traces: accepted directly when the schema and version are supported.
- Sampled traces: accepted with metadata describing sampling method, time window, and scale-up assumptions.
- Workload summaries: accepted by generating synthetic replay workloads from arrival, sequence-length, session, and cache-locality distributions.
- Raw traces: accepted only through supported conversion/validation tooling, not silently interpreted by the profiler.

The minimum dynamic workload contract should be payload-free and include enough information for Replay to simulate arrival dynamics and cache behavior. For trace-style inputs, each record should include timestamp or inter-arrival time, model or deployment target, input token count, requested or observed output token count, request class or priority when applicable, session/turn identifiers for multi-turn traffic when applicable, and prefix/cache identity metadata such as trace block hashes when available. For summary-style inputs, the contract should include the time window, request-rate or concurrency distribution, input/output token distributions, model mix, session/multi-turn distribution, cache locality or prefix-sharing distribution, and optional request priority/SLA classes.

To make dynamic workload input usable, Dynamo should add a trace capture and export path. The frontend, or a frontend-adjacent admin tool, should be able to record payload-free request metadata, redact or omit user content, export a Replay-ready or converter-ready artifact to a PVC/object-store location, and emit a reference that a DGDR can consume. A companion validator/converter should tell users whether a raw or sampled trace can be used as-is, must be converted, or is missing fields.

The profiler will translate the DGDR into a search space covering engine configuration, router configuration, and planner configuration. DGDR owns generating and searching these knobs:

- Engine: `backend`, `backend_version`, `tp_size`, `moe_tp_size`, `moe_ep_size`, `attention_dp_size`, `kv_block_size`.
- Router: all router configuration fields.
- Planner: all planner configuration fields except SLA inputs, which remain user-owned constraints.

Users may still pin any generated knob through DGDR constraints. Pinned values reduce the search space and are reported as binding constraints. Generated values can be auto-applied only when the DGDR policy allows it and the candidate passes all safety checks; otherwise they are advisory recommendations.

Before executing Replay, the profiler must preflight and filter candidates. Preflight should remove candidates that fail memory fit, backend support, SKU/hardware support, GPU budget, recipe constraints, image/runtime compatibility, or user-pinned constraints. AIC remains the owner for memory estimation. The profiler owns the remaining feasibility checks and should report skipped candidates with structured reasons.

For each viable candidate, the profiler will invoke Replay rather than directly estimating static throughput. Replay will use AIC forward-pass estimates for engine timing and will simulate the surrounding Dynamo deployment behavior, including scheduler behavior, multiple replicas, router decisions, planner interactions, and request arrival dynamics. Because Replay is CPU-based and deterministic under fixed seeds, the profiler can run many trials in parallel.

Use Google Vizier as the initial black-box optimizer for the search loop. The optimizer objective is to find configurations that satisfy the requested SLA, or, when cost constraints are provided, to optimize SLA/cost tradeoffs. The profiler should keep the best candidate and ranked alternatives instead of returning only one result.

The DGDR output contract should include:

- A ranked list of viable candidates, with the selected candidate first.
- Generated DGD for each returned candidate.
- Generated router configuration for each returned candidate.
- Generated planner configuration for each returned candidate.
- Replay report or replay report reference for each returned candidate.
- Ranked alternative candidates with their scores and SLA/cost metrics.
- Binding constraints that limited the search.
- Skipped and failed candidate reasons.
- Warnings and confidence indicators for the recommendation.
- Recommendation mode: advisory or auto-applied.

This proposal assumes AIC can provide forward-pass estimates for all targeted models: kernel-level estimates for profiled models, and forward-pass-level estimates for new models through online onboarding once available. If AIC support is incomplete for a model/configuration, fallback must be explicit and safe: use only recipe-backed or fit-proven alternatives, otherwise fail fast with `NoViableCandidate`. The profiler must not silently use naive or unproven fallbacks.

## Alternate Solutions

A1. If AIC forward-pass online onboarding is not ready for a model, use only recipe-backed or fit-proven alternatives. The fallback must be explicit in the DGDR status and must carry lower confidence than a fully AIC-backed candidate.

A2. Fail fast with `NoViableCandidate` when neither AIC nor a recipe-backed/fit-proven fallback can support the requested model, hardware, backend, and constraints.

A3. Use AIBroom instead of Google Vizier for smart search. This may be preferable if it better fits existing AIC optimization flows, but Vizier is proposed first because it provides a general black-box optimization interface for mixed configuration spaces.

A4. Keep planner linear-regression FPM modeling as an implicit fallback. This is rejected because silent naive fallbacks are one of the current DGDR UX problems; unsupported candidates should be skipped with reasons or fail fast.

## Requirements

- DGDR profiling MUST preserve the existing DGDR-based user workflow.
- DGDR profiling MUST support existing static traffic inputs.
- DGDR profiling SHOULD add dynamic traffic input through trace references, sampled traces, workload summaries, or replay-ready workload artifacts.
- DGDR profiling MUST normalize dynamic workload inputs into a Replay-ready workload contract before executing Replay.
- DGDR profiling SHOULD provide frontend or frontend-adjacent tooling to record, validate, convert, and link payload-free traces for DGDR input.
- AIC MUST provide a forward-pass estimation API usable by Replay for candidate evaluation.
- AIC MUST remain the source of memory-fit estimation.
- AIC SHOULD support both profiled models and newly onboarded models.
- Replay MUST expose a stable programmatic API for DGDR profiler sweeps.
- Replay MUST support deterministic CPU-based evaluation under fixed seeds.
- Replay MUST support engine, router, and planner configuration inputs in the same candidate trial.
- Replay SHOULD return structured metrics suitable for SLA and SLA/cost optimization.
- The profiler MUST construct and validate the search space before launching trials.
- The profiler MUST preflight candidates for memory fit, backend support, SKU/hardware support, GPU budget, recipe constraints, image/runtime compatibility, and user-pinned constraints before invoking Replay.
- The profiler MUST report skipped and failed candidate reasons.
- The profiler SHOULD run Replay trials in parallel.
- The profiler SHOULD return a ranked candidate list with generated DGD, router config, planner config, replay report or replay report reference, binding constraints, warnings/confidence, and recommendation mode.
- The profiler MUST return multiple viable candidates when multiple candidates pass the objective and safety checks.
- The profiler MUST fail with `NoViableCandidate` when no AIC-backed or recipe-backed/fit-proven candidate can satisfy the request.
- The profiler MUST NOT silently use naive fallback performance models.
- The implementation MUST avoid duplicating forward-pass modeling logic outside AIC.
- The implementation MUST avoid duplicating deployment simulation logic outside Replay.

## References

- Dynamo Replay docs: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/mocker-trace-replay.md
- Dynamo mocker docs: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/main/docs/mocker/mocker.md
- Planner replay benchmarking docs: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/planner-replay-benchmarking.md
- Dynamo PR #7553: feat(mocker): add multi-worker replay and router startup fixes
- Dynamo PR #7593: feat(replay): add shared loadgen workload paths
- Dynamo PR #7729: test(replay): compare offline replay against AIC static point
- Dynamo PR #7774: feat(replay): add agg/disagg offline replay optimization
- Dynamo PR #8187: feat(replay): planner-in-the-loop offline replay
- Dynamo PR #8195: docs(profiler): add replay_optimize sweep README
- Dynamo PR #8280: fix(replay/planner): planner-in-the-loop replay diagnostics and planner scaling fixes
- Dynamo PR #8518: feat(profiler): add replay objective knob
- Dynamo PR #8585: chore(profiler): reshape replay_optimize into DGDR-aligned Pydantic specs
- Dynamo PR #8641: docs(planner): add planner replay benchmarking guide
- AIConfigurator PR #981: feat: add AIC Rust core forward-pass estimator
- AIConfigurator PR #665: feat(sdk): add static latency-only fast path
- AIConfigurator PR #361 / #419: hook to Dynamo planner profiler config generation

items.title: fix(mocker): make KVBM allocation and offload lifecycle race-free [DYN-3299]
items.body:
## Overview:

Make mocker G1 allocation and KVBM-driven offload progression transactional at their observable boundaries. Ordinary allocation either commits completely or remains invisible; externally triggered pipeline completions settle through successor invocation; and mocker-owned offload resources remain leased until child registration and router visibility are acknowledged.

This combines the immediate scheduler-fidelity correction from #11016, the semaphore-handoff settlement slice of #11018, the replay-liveness integration from #11015, and the mocker lease-coordinator follow-up reviewed in #11031.

## Details:

### Transactional scheduler allocation

- Make each VLLM `MoveBlock::Use` an all-or-nothing prepare/reserve/commit transaction.
- Propagate typed capacity, concrete offload-dependency, and bounded immediate-retry outcomes through admission, ordinary and speculative decode, destination reservation, and swap-in.
- Prevent failed attempts from publishing phantom cache entries, partial active references, prefix credit, registration, or `Stored` events.

### Linearized KVBM pipeline settlement

- Add one linearized snapshot per pipeline plus settlement token/target APIs.
- Acknowledge drained batches only after immediately runnable successors have invoked their workers.
- Publish structured terminal failures for cancellation, abort, panic, executor error, channel closure, stale tokens, unavailable lanes, and overflow.
- Preserve live KVBM scheduling and concurrency; real live users do not call settlement.

### Mocker-owned offload leases

- Centralize G1→G2, G2→G3, G2→G4, direct swap-in, and staged swap-in ownership in a crate-private generational coordinator.
- Retain the original pre-enqueue G3/G4 checkpoint across cross-owner drains and settle cumulative deferred deltas against it.
- Finalize in two phases: settle and prepare progress, register child leases and collect lifecycle events, publish router visibility, then acknowledge before releasing source slots or tier reservations.
- Replace swap-in completion flags with structured watch status while the coordinator owns destination slots, prefix/source pins, reservations, handles, cancellation state, and terminal failures.
- Keep request cancellation rigorous while mocker is active without adding process-exit graceful-shutdown behavior.

### Replay liveness boundary

- Preserve the balanced zero-duration progress gate: stop same-timestamp spinning without misclassifying unfinished work as quiescent.
- Disable wall-clock request expiry only for offline replay; live routing retains its five-minute TTL.
- Keep modeled deadlines and command-triggered eviction anchored to command application time.

Lifecycle watermarks and generalized auto-chain closure remain deferred in #11018.

## Where should the reviewer start?

1. `lib/mocker/src/kv_manager/kvbm_backend.rs` for the transactional `prepare_use`/commit boundary and typed dependency outcomes.
2. `lib/kvbm-engine/src/offload/pipeline.rs` and the settlement types under `lib/kvbm-engine/src/offload/` for the linearized pipeline contract.
3. `lib/mocker/src/kvbm_offload/coordinator.rs` for lease ownership, retained shared-lane checkpoints, and prepare/acknowledge finalization.
4. `lib/mocker/src/kvbm_offload/engine.rs` for settlement sequencing, child registration, router-event preparation, and acknowledgement-time release.
5. `lib/mocker/src/scheduler/vllm/core.rs` for scheduler integration and cancellation behavior.

## Related Issues

- Relates to #11015.
- Relates to #11016.
- Relates to #11018.
- Incorporates merged stacked PR #11031.
- Linear: [DYN-3299](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-3299/make-mocker-g1-allocation-and-kvbm-settlement-race-free).

## Validation

### Correctness and flake gates

Initial settlement candidate `76e1d7afb7e4b7733e8e76bde6d3ca081c068094` on an SC-01 CPU-only x86_64 allocation:

- complete `kvbm-engine`: 125 passed
- complete `kvbm-logical`: 493 passed plus 3 doctests
- `cargo test --locked -p dynamo-mocker --features kvbm-offload`: 557 passed, 1 ignored
- full mocker feature suite: 20/20 clean repetitions
- `idle_destination_reservation_wakes_at_offload_deadline`: 200/200 repetitions
- `live_destination_eviction_uses_command_application_time`: 200/200 repetitions

Lease-coordinator follow-up:

- complete `cargo test --locked -p dynamo-mocker`
- complete `cargo test --locked -p dynamo-mocker --features kvbm-offload`
- focused unchanged-core `kvbm-engine` settlement tests
- full KVBM feature suite: 20/20 clean repetitions
- both known semaphore regressions: 200/200 repetitions each
- `cargo clippy --no-deps --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --check`

Deterministic coverage includes concurrency one and greater than one, simultaneous completions, no successor, progress between subscription and initial check, block/object executors, cross-owner G3/G4 drains, cumulative deferred waves, partial chains, direct/staged cancellation, task abort, panic, executor error, channel closure, stale/foreign acknowledgements, and exactly-once slot/reservation release.

### White-box and semantic parity

Temporary tracing was applied only in Computelab scratch checkouts and removed before performance collection. It verified settlement-token capture, expected per-lane deltas, snapshot transitions, permit release and successor invocation, router publication before acknowledgement, source-slot release, and zero final live leases or stranded modeled work.

- Control and G2-only traces matched exactly apart from the intended source-slot release correction.
- Lower-tier traces preserved outputs, completion order, transfer counts, router decisions, and final drained state.
- The remaining lower-tier delta was the accepted two-phase lifetime correction: 12 final HostPinned removals were retained past the comparison boundary, and removal timestamps moved until child registration and router publication were acknowledged.
- No unexplained semantic difference remained.

### Performance

Initial seven-pair live A/B:

- control throughput median **-0.141%**; p95 latency **+0.132%**
- offload-heavy throughput median **-0.453%**; p95 latency **+0.479%**
- all 28 measured runs completed with 100% successful requests and no output-length mismatch

Lease-refactor replay A/B:

- control workload throughput median **+0.293%**
- offload-heavy workload throughput median **+0.446%**

All agreed performance gates passed.

### Aggressive-tracing observation

With an intentionally tiny 12-block G1, concurrency four, and aggressive debug tracing, requests could not coexist once tracing stretched their overlap. The scheduler entered 122,879 preempt/requeue passes and seven clients timed out; the identical normal-logging workload completed 24/24 exact outputs in order. The capacity preemption is expected for that artificial setup; the tight spin remains a broader scheduler yield/backoff concern rather than a pipeline-settlement or lease-coordinator regression.

items.body:
## What

Extracts the chat-template / prompt-formatting engine out of `lib/llm` into a new standalone, runtime-free **`dynamo-renderer`** crate, so it can be reused by an external OpenAI frontend (e.g. an SGLang Rust HTTP server) without pulling in the Dynamo runtime.

- New `dynamo-renderer` crate: owns the `OAIChatLikeRequest` trait, HF `chat_template` rendering (minijinja + pycompat), and native DeepSeek formatters (under `deepseek/`). Ships the ready-made impl for `dynamo-protocols`' OpenAI chat request (orphan-rule-legal here since the trait is local). Re-exports `dynamo-tokenizers` as a one-import convenience. Includes `README.md` + `CLAUDE.md` (`AGENTS.md` symlink) matching sibling crates.
- `dynamo-tokenizers` stays a pure tokenization leaf — no protocols, no minijinja, no feature flags.
- `dynamo-protocols` stays a pure wire-types leaf.
- `lib/llm` depends on `dynamo-renderer`; `crate::preprocessor::prompt` keeps only the lib/llm-local glue (`Nv*` impls, the `MediaRequestExt` extension trait, `prompt_formatter_from_mdc`). Everything else imports `dynamo_renderer` directly — no back-compat re-exports. `PromptContextMixin` moves to the crate.

```
dynamo-protocols (wire types, leaf)     dynamo-tokenizers (tokenize, leaf)
                 \                       /
                  dynamo-renderer  (trait + engine + impl; re-exports tokenizers)
                         |
                      dynamo-llm  (Nv* impls, MediaRequestExt, prompt_formatter_from_mdc)
```

## Why a separate crate — and the approach we tried first

The motivating goal was "let an external Rust frontend reuse our chat templating." The first attempt was to **fold the prompt code into `dynamo-tokenizers`** behind a `chat-template` feature — the reasoning being that HF's `apply_chat_template` is a method *on the tokenizer* and the template ships in `tokenizer_config.json`, so it felt conceptually adjacent.

That turned out to be the wrong home, for one concrete reason: **the renderer imports nothing from the tokenizer side of the crate** — it never touches encode/decode/vocab. The only thing binding the two together was the mental model, not the code. The renderer is really a *bridge* between OpenAI request types (`dynamo-protocols`) and the HF jinja engine (`minijinja`).

Forcing it into `dynamo-tokenizers` bought zero code-sharing and created a pile of dependency/feature gymnastics we wanted to avoid:

- **A `tokenizers -> protocols` dependency edge.** The default `OAIChatLikeRequest` impl is for `dynamo_protocols::types::CreateChatCompletionRequest`, and the trait's `typed_messages()` returned a `dynamo_protocols` type. So the "lean leaf" tokenizer crate had to depend (even optionally) on the wire-protocol crate — backwards layering for the most foundational crate, which is also consumed by KV routing / token counting that never touch OpenAI types.
- **A `chat-template` Cargo feature on `dynamo-tokenizers`** (plus `serde_json/preserve_order`, `serde_json/raw_value`, optional `minijinja`/`chrono`/`either`/`dynamo-protocols`) just to keep the default build lean. Feature-gating a whole second persona onto a single-purpose crate.
- **The orphan rule made every alternative awkward.** `impl OAIChatLikeRequest for CreateChatCompletionRequest` can only live in the crate that owns the trait *or* the type. With the trait in tokenizers, that meant either keeping the `tokenizers -> protocols` edge, or inverting it (`protocols` gains a `chat-template` feature that depends on `tokenizers` and hosts the impl) — which then needs a **dev-dependency cycle** so the tokenizer crate's own tests can still construct the protocol type. A third "glue" crate couldn't host the impl at all without a newtype wrapper, which is exactly the wrapper friction external consumers were trying to avoid.

Giving the bridge its own crate dissolves all of it: the trait lives in `dynamo-renderer`, so the protocol impl is local-trait-legal; both leaf crates go back to having a single job and zero feature flags; and dependencies flow one direction only.

## Why "renderer"

The crate is the *encode* half of converting between structured chat (messages + tools) and what the model sees. The natural counterpart is the *decode* half — parsing model output back into reasoning / tool calls — which already lives in `dynamo-parsers`. Naming this `dynamo-renderer` positions it as the encode side of that pairing (cf. the "renderers" concept), leaving room to grow a bidirectional `Renderer` abstraction later that composes render + parse + tokenize.

## Testing

- `dynamo-renderer`: 87 tests. `dynamo-tokenizers`: 37 (lean). `dynamo-llm`: 1137 lib unit + `deepseek_v4`/`v32` integration (12 + 4) pass. clippy + fmt clean across all three.
- Python bindings rebuilt via `maturin develop` against the new crate graph.
- **E2E on 2x L40S** (`dynamo.frontend` + `dynamo.sglang`, Qwen3-0.6B): multi-turn `/no_think` renders correctly (`<think>\n\n</think>\n\nParis.`, finish=stop); tool-calling turn renders the tools section and emits a valid Qwen `<tool_call>` for `get_weather(city=Paris)`.

> Note: `lib/llm/tests/preprocessor.rs` has tests that download the gated `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct` config and fail with HTTP 401 without an HF token for that repo. Those failures are environmental and reproduce on a clean `main`; the non-gated tests in that file pass.

items.title: [BUG]: TTFT degradation with KVBM + MTP enabled in Dynamo 0.9.0  (TRTLLM with DeepSeek-R1)
items.body:
### Describe the Bug

We tried to run aggregated inference with DeepSeek-R1 using Dynamo 0.9.0 and observed that enabling KVBM together with MTP does not behave as expected.

Specifically, when MTP is enabled on top of KVBM, median TTFT increases significantly, despite improvements in decode throughput and overall E2E latency.

Environment:

- Dynamo version: 0.9.0
- TensorRT-LLM version: 1.3.0-rc1
- Model: DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4-v2
- Benchmarking tool: follow the [doc](https://docs.nvidia.com/dynamo/dev/components/kvbm/kvbm-guide#benchmarking-kvbm) to use LMBenchmark.

Comparison between:

- KVBM only
- KVBM  + MTP 3

Metrics were collected from the inference metrics endpoint (port 6880) and Dynamo (port 9090). We can see once MTP is enabled, Median TTFT become worse.

| Metric                     | KVBM Only | KVBM + MTP 3 |
|----------------------------|-----------|------------|
| Total requests             | 365       | 464        |
| Avg E2E latency            | ~11.98 s  | ~9.21 s    |
| Median E2E latency         | ~10–15 s  | ~5–10 s    |
| Avg TTFT                   | ~1.77 s   | ~4.66 s    |
| Median TTFT                | ~0.5–0.75 s | ~5–7.5 s |
| Avg ITL                    | ~0.103 s  | ~0.046 s   |
| Median ITL                 | ~0.10–0.15 s | ~0.05 s |
| Tokens/sec (decode)        | ~9.7 tok/s | ~21–22 tok/s |
| Avg queue time             | ~1.42 s   | ~2.94 s    |
| Median queue time          | ≤0.3 s    | ~2.5–5 s   |
| Host KV hit                | 47.3%     | 39.4%      |
| Disk KV hit                | 10.6%     | 22.2%      |

### Steps to Reproduce

Deployment config file. Please be notice that fraction is set as 0.09 to trigger the KVBM.
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: deepseek-r1-fp4-c
data:
  engine-config.yaml: |
    tensor_parallel_size: 8
    moe_expert_parallel_size: 8
    gpus_per_node: 8

    enable_attention_dp: false

    max_batch_size: 128
    max_num_tokens: 80000
    max_seq_len: 163840
    enable_chunked_prefill: false

    stream_interval: 10

    # Follow example to disable CUDA graph. For cache hit rate, no difference between enable and disable.
    # cuda_graph_config:
    #   enable_padding: true
    #   max_batch_size: 128
    cuda_graph_config: null

    # Default backend is CUTLASS, we could explore if TRTLLM works better
    moe_config:
      backend: TRTLLM

    # default is pytorch
    # backend: pytorch
    kv_cache_config:
      dtype: fp8
      # Lower threshold to trigger KVBM offloading earlier (0.2 = 20% GPU memory for KV cache)
      free_gpu_memory_fraction: 0.09
      # NOTE: enable_block_reuse is TRT-LLM's native feature - must NOT be present for KVBM
      # Recommended by Dynamo to disable this to increase offloading cache hits
      enable_partial_reuse: false
      # enable_block_reuse: true

    kv_connector_config:
      connector_module: kvbm.trtllm_integration.connector
      connector_scheduler_class: DynamoKVBMConnectorLeader
      connector_worker_class: DynamoKVBMConnectorWorker

    # NOTE: MTP (speculative decoding) is NOT compatible with KVBM
    speculative_config:
      decoding_type: MTP
      num_nextn_predict_layers: 3
---
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: DynamoGraphDeployment
metadata:
  name: deepseek-r1-fp4-c
spec:
  services:
    Frontend:
      dynamoNamespace: deepseek-r1-fp4-c
      componentType: frontend
      replicas: 1
      extraPodSpec:
        imagePullSecrets:
          - name: ecr-886436935921
        mainContainer:
          image: nvcr.io/nvidia/ai-dynamo/tensorrtllm-runtime:0.9.0
      envs:
        - name: DYN_ROUTER_MODE
          value: kv
    TRTLLMWorker:
      envFromSecret: hf-token-secret
      dynamoNamespace: deepseek-r1-fp4-c
      componentType: worker
      replicas: 1
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "32"
          memory: 256Gi
          gpu: "8"
        limits:
          cpu: "64"
          memory: 512Gi
          gpu: "8"
      envs:
        - name: DYN_KVBM_CPU_CACHE_GB
          value: "64"
        - name: DYN_KVBM_DISK_CACHE_GB
          value: "64"
        - name: DYN_KVBM_LEADER_WORKER_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS
          value: "1200"
        - name: DYN_KVBM_TRTLLM_ZMQ_PORT
          value: "20081"
        - name: DYN_KVBM_DISABLE_DISK_OFFLOAD_FILTER
          value: "true"
        - name: DYN_KVBM_METRICS
          value: "true"
        - name: HF_HOME
          value: "/model-cache"
        - name: HF_HUB_CACHE
          value: "/model-cache/hub"
        - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
          value: "0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7"
        # - name: DYN_LOG
        #   value: "debug"
        # - name: RUST_LOG
        #   value: "kvbm=debug,dynamo_llm=debug"
      extraPodSpec:
        imagePullSecrets:
          - name: ecr-886436935921
        runtimeClassName: nvidia
        nodeSelector:
          sandbox: "true"
          # Pin to specific node for hostPath weights cache
          kubernetes.io/hostname: hydra-texas-b200-17
        tolerations:
          - key: "sandbox"
            operator: "Equal"
            value: "true"
            effect: "NoSchedule"
          - key: "nvidia.com/gpu"
            operator: "Exists"
            effect: "NoSchedule"
        volumes:
          - name: engine-config
            configMap:
              name: deepseek-r1-fp4-c
          - name: model-cache
            hostPath:
              path: /mnt/model-cache/deepseek-r1-fp4
              type: DirectoryOrCreate
        mainContainer:
          image: nvcr.io/nvidia/ai-dynamo/tensorrtllm-runtime:0.9.0
          workingDir: /workspace/
          volumeMounts:
            - name: engine-config
              mountPath: /config
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /model-cache
          command:
            - "/bin/bash"
            - "-c"
          args:
            - |
              python -m dynamo.trtllm \
                --model-path nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4-v2 \
                --served-model-name nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4-v2 \
                --gpus-per-node 8 \
                --max-num-tokens 80000 \
                --max-batch-size 128 \
                --extra-engine-args /config/engine-config.yaml \
                --publish-events-and-metrics

```

Run benchmark tool:
```
python multi-round-qa.py \
    --model nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4-v2 \
    --base-url https://ai.cloud.modular.com:32443 \
    --shared-system-prompt 8000 \
    --user-history-prompt 50000 \
    --answer-len 100 \
    --num-users 5 \
    --num-rounds 150 \
    --qps 5.0 \
    --time 900 \
    --enforce-strict-concurrent-users \
    --output kvbm_extreme_test.csv
```

### Expected Behavior

When enabling MTP together with KVBM, we expect:

- improved decode throughput due to speculative decoding.
- TTFT to remain comparable to KVBM-only runs, or increase only marginally, since speculative decoding primarily affects the decode phase rather than prefill.
- No significant increase in request queue time or scheduling latency.
- Overall end-to-end latency to remain similar or improve due to faster decode throughput.

The substantial TTFT regression observed with KVBM + MTP was therefore unexpected.

### Actual Behavior

When enabling MTP  together with KVBM, we observed a significant degradation in TTFT compared to running with KVBM only.

Specifically:

- Median TTFT increased substantially (approximately ~0.5–0.75 s with KVBM only vs ~5–7.5 s with KVBM + MTP).
- Average TTFT also increased (~1.77 s → ~4.66 s).
- Request queue time increased noticeably when MTP was enabled (median ≤0.3 s → ~2.5–5 s).

At the same time:

- Decode throughput improved significantly (~9.7 tok/s → ~21–22 tok/s).
- Average E2E latency decreased (~11.98 s → ~9.21 s).
- KV cache hit distribution shifted (host hit rate decreased, disk hit rate increased).

Overall, enabling MTP alongside KVBM resulted in improved decode throughput but unexpectedly caused substantial TTFT regression and increased queueing latency.

### Environment

Environment:

- Dynamo version: 0.9.0
- TensorRT-LLM version: 1.3.0-rc1
- Model: DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4-v2
- Benchmarking tool: follow the [doc](https://docs.nvidia.com/dynamo/dev/components/kvbm/kvbm-guide#benchmarking-kvbm) to use LMBenchmark.


### Additional Context
